{{Short description|Distance between two metric-space subsets}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Hausdorff distance''', or '''Hausdorff metric''', also called '''Pompeiu–Hausdorff distance''',<ref name="rock">{{cite book |author-link=R. Tyrrell Rockafellar |first1=R. Tyrrell |last1=Rockafellar |author-link2=Roger J-B Wets |first2=Roger J-B |last2=Wets |title=Variational Analysis |publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=2005 |isbn=3-540-62772-3 |page=117 }}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last1=Bîrsan|first1=Temistocle|contribution=One hundred years since the introduction of the set distance by Dimitrie Pompeiu| year=2006|title=System Modeling and Optimization|volume=199|pages=35–39|editor-last=Ceragioli|editor-first=Francesca|place=Boston|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Kluwer Academic Publishers]]|language=en|doi=10.1007/0-387-33006-2_4|isbn=978-0-387-32774-7|last2=Tiba|first2=Dan|editor2-last=Dontchev|editor2-first=Asen|editor3-last=Futura|editor3-first=Hitoshi|editor4-last=Marti|editor4-first=Kurt|editor5-last=Pandolfi|editor5-first=Luciano|mr=2249320|doi-access=free}}
</ref> measures how far two [[subset]]s of a [[metric space]] are from each other. It turns the set of [[non-empty set|non-empty]] [[compact space|compact]] subsets of a metric space into a metric space in its own right. It is named after [[Felix Hausdorff]] and [[Dimitrie Pompeiu]].

Informally, two sets are close in the Hausdorff distance if every point of either set is close to some point of the other set. The Hausdorff distance is the longest distance someone can be forced to travel by an adversary who chooses a point in one of the two sets, from where they then must travel to the other set. In other words, it is the greatest of all the distances from a point in one set to the closest point in the other set.

This distance was first introduced by Hausdorff in his book ''[[Grundzüge der Mengenlehre]]'', first published in 1914, although a very close relative appeared in the doctoral thesis of [[Maurice René Fréchet|Maurice Fréchet]] in 1906, in his study of the space of all continuous curves from <math>[0,1] \to \R^3</math>.

==Definition==
[[Image:Hausdorff distance sample.svg|thumb|250px|right|Components of the calculation of the Hausdorff distance between the green curve ''X'' and the blue curve ''Y''.]]

Let <math display="inline">(M,d)</math> be a [[metric space]]. For each pair of non-empty subsets <math display="inline">X \subset M</math> and <math display="inline">Y \subset M</math>, the Hausdorff distance between <math display="inline">X</math> and <math>Y</math> is defined as

<math display="block"> d_{\mathrm H}(X,Y) := \max\left\{\,\sup_{x \in X} d(x,Y),\ \sup_{y \in Y} d(X,y) \,\right\},</math>

where <math display="inline">\operatorname{sup}</math> represents the [[supremum]] operator, <math display="inline">d(a, B) := \displaystyle\inf_{b \in B} d(a,b)</math> quantifies the distance from a point <math display="inline">a \in X</math> to the subset <math display="inline">B\subseteq X</math>, and <math display="inline">\operatorname{inf}</math> is the [[infimum]] operator.

An equivalent definition is as follows.<ref>{{cite book |last=Munkres |first=James |author-link=James Munkres|title=Topology |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Prentice Hall]] |year=1999 |isbn=0-13-181629-2 |pages=280–281 |url={{Google books |plainurl=yes |id=XjoZAQAAIAAJ |page=280 }} }}</ref> For each set <math>X \subset M,</math> let 
<math display="block"> 
X_\varepsilon := \bigcup_{x \in X} \{z \in M \mid  d(z,x) < \varepsilon\},
</math>
which is the set of all points within <math display="inline">\varepsilon</math> of the set <math display="inline">X</math> (sometimes called the <math display="inline">\varepsilon</math>-fattening of <math display="inline">X</math> or a generalized [[Ball (mathematics)|ball]] of radius <math display="inline">\varepsilon</math> around <math display="inline">X</math>).
Then, the Hausdorff distance between <math display="inline">X</math> and <math display="inline">Y</math> is defined as 
<math display="block"> 
d_\mathrm{H}(X,Y) := \inf\{\varepsilon \geq 0 \mid X \subseteq Y_\varepsilon \text{ and } Y \subseteq X_\varepsilon\}.
</math>

Equivalently,<ref name="rock"/>
<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
d_\mathrm{H}(X, Y) &= \sup_{w \in M} \left| \inf_{x \in X} d(w,x) - \inf_{y \in Y} d(w,y)\right| \\ [6px]
&= \sup_{w \in X \cup Y} \left| \inf_{x \in X} d(w,x) - \inf_{y \in Y} d(w,y)\right| \\ [6px]
&= \sup_{w \in M} \bigl| d(w, X) - d(w, Y)\bigr|.
\end{aligned} 
</math>

===Remark===

It is not true for arbitrary subsets <math display="inline">X, Y \subset M</math> that <math display="inline"> d_{\mathrm H}(X,Y) = \varepsilon </math> implies <math display="inline"> X\subseteq Y_\varepsilon </math> and <math display="inline">Y\subseteq X_\varepsilon.</math>

For instance, consider the metric space of the real numbers <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}</math> with the usual metric <math>d</math> induced by the absolute value,

<math display="block">d(x,y) := |y - x|, \qquad x,y \in \R.</math>

Take

<math display="block">X := (0, 1] \quad \mbox{and} \quad Y := [-1,0). </math>

Then <math display="inline">d_{\mathrm H}(X,Y) = 1\ </math>. However <math display="inline">X \nsubseteq Y_1</math> because <math>Y_1 = (-2,1)</math>, but <math display="inline">1 \in X</math>.

But it is true that
:<math> X \subseteq \{x \in M \,{:}\, d(x, Y) \leq \varepsilon\}</math>&emsp;and&emsp;<math> Y \subseteq \{x \in M \,{:}\, d(x, X) \leq \varepsilon\}</math>;
in particular it is true if <math display="inline">X</math> and <math display="inline">Y</math> are closed.

==Properties==
* In general, <math>d_\text{H}(X, Y)</math> may be infinite. If both ''X'' and ''Y'' are [[bounded set|bounded]], then <math>d_\text{H}(X, Y)</math> is guaranteed to be finite.
* <math>d_\text{H}(X, Y) = 0</math> if and only if ''X'' and ''Y'' have the same closure.
* For every point ''x'' of ''M'' and any non-empty sets ''Y'', ''Z'' of ''M'': ''d''(''x'',&nbsp;''Y'') ≤ ''d''(''x'',&nbsp;''Z'') + ''d''<sub>H</sub>(''Y'',&nbsp;''Z''), where  ''d''(''x'',&nbsp;''Y'') is the distance between the point ''x'' and the closest point in the set ''Y''.
* |diameter(''Y'') − diameter(''X'')| ≤ 2''d''<sub>H</sub>(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'').<ref>[https://math.stackexchange.com/q/375296 Diameter and Hausdorff Distance], Math.SE.</ref>
* If the intersection ''X''&nbsp;∩&nbsp;''Y'' has a non-empty interior, then there exists a constant ''r''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, such that every set ''X''′ whose Hausdorff distance from ''X'' is less than ''r'' also intersects ''Y''.<ref>[https://math.stackexchange.com/q/732850 Hausdorff Distance and Intersection], Math.SE.</ref>
* On the set of all subsets of ''M'', ''d''<sub>H</sub> yields an extended [[pseudometric space|pseudometric]].
* On the set ''F''(''M'') of all non-empty compact subsets of ''M'', ''d''<sub>H</sub> is a metric.
** If ''M'' is [[complete metric space|complete]], then so is ''F''(''M'').<ref>{{cite journal |title=Completeness and total boundedness of the Hausdorff metric |first=Jeff |last=Henrikson |journal=MIT Undergraduate Journal of Mathematics |year=1999 |pages=69–80 |url=http://www-math.mit.edu/phase2/UJM/vol1/HAUSF.PDF |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020623095720/http://www-math.mit.edu/phase2/UJM/vol1/HAUSF.PDF |archive-date=June 23, 2002 }}</ref>
** If ''M'' is compact, then so is ''F''(''M'').
** The [[topological space|topology]] of ''F''(''M'') depends only on the topology of ''M'', not on the metric ''d''.

==Motivation==
The definition of the Hausdorff distance can be derived by a series of natural extensions of the distance function <math>d(x,y)</math> in the underlying metric space ''M'', as follows:<ref>{{cite book
  | last = Barnsley
  | first = Michael
  | author-link = Michael Barnsley
  | title = Fractals Everywhere
  | publisher = [[Morgan Kaufmann Publishers|Morgan Kaufmann]]
  | year = 1993
  | pages = Ch. II.6
  | isbn = 0-12-079069-6}}
</ref>
* Define a distance function between any point ''x'' of ''M'' and any non-empty set ''Y'' of ''M'' by <math display="block>
 d(x, Y) = \inf\{d(x, y) \mid y \in Y\}.
</math> For example, ''d''(1, {3, 6}) = 2 and ''d''(7, {3, 6}) = 1.
* Define a (not necessarily symmetric) "distance" function between any two non-empty sets ''X'' and ''Y'' of ''M'' by <math display="block>
 d(X, Y) = \sup\{d(x, Y) \mid x \in X\}.
</math> For example, <math>d(\{1, 7\}, \{3, 6\}) = \sup\{d(1, \{3, 6\}), d(7, \{3, 6\})\} = \sup\{d(1, 3), d(7, 6)\} = 2.</math>
* If ''X'' and ''Y'' are compact, then ''d''(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'') will be finite; ''d''(''X'',&nbsp;''X'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0; and ''d'' inherits the [[triangle inequality]] property from the distance function in ''M''. As it stands,  ''d''(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'') is ''not'' a metric because ''d''(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'') is not always symmetric, and {{nowrap|1=''d''(''X'', ''Y'') = 0}} does not imply that {{nowrap|1=''X'' = ''Y''}} (it does imply that <math>X \subseteq \overline{Y}</math>). For example, {{nowrap|1=''d''({1, 3, 6, 7}, {3, 6}) = 2}}, but {{nowrap|1=''d''({3, 6}, {1, 3, 6, 7}) = 0}}. However, we can create a metric by defining the Hausdorff distance to be <math display="block">
 d_\text{H}(X, Y) = \max\{d(X, Y), d(Y, X)\}.
</math>

==Applications==
In [[computer vision]], the Hausdorff distance can be used to find a given template in an arbitrary target image. The template and image are often pre-processed via an [[Edge detection|edge detector]] giving a [[binary image]]. Next, each 1 (activated) point in the binary image of the template is treated as a point in a set, the "shape" of the template. Similarly, an area of the binary target image is treated as a set of points. The algorithm then tries to minimize the Hausdorff distance between the template and some area of the target image. The area in the target image with the minimal Hausdorff distance to the template, can be considered the best candidate for locating the template in the target.
In [[computer graphics]] the Hausdorff distance is used to measure the difference between two different representations of the same 3D object<ref>{{cite journal |first1=P. |last1=Cignoni |first2=C. |last2=Rocchini |first3=R. |last3=Scopigno |title=Metro: Measuring Error on Simplified Surfaces |journal=Computer Graphics Forum |volume=17 |issue=2 |year=1998 |pages=167–174 |doi=10.1111/1467-8659.00236 |s2cid=17783159 }}</ref> particularly when generating [[Level of detail (computer graphics)|level of detail]] for efficient display of complex 3D models.

[[File:Oceanic_pole_of_inaccessibility.png|thumb|Oceanic pole of inaccessibility at {{Coord|49.0273|S|123.4345|W|name=Oceanic Pole of Inaccessibility}}]]
If <math>X</math> is the surface of Earth, and <math>Y</math> is the land-surface of Earth, then by finding the [[Pole of inaccessibility#Oceanic pole of inaccessibility|point Nemo]], we see <math>d_\text{H}(X, Y)</math> is around 2,704.8&nbsp;km.

==Related concepts==
A measure for the dissimilarity of two shapes is given by ''Hausdorff distance up to isometry'', denoted ''D''<sub>H</sub>. Namely, let ''X'' and ''Y'' be two compact figures in a metric space ''M'' (usually a [[Euclidean space]]); then ''D''<sub>H</sub>(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'') is the infimum of ''d''<sub>H</sub>(''I''(''X''),&nbsp;''Y'') among all [[isometry|isometries]] ''I'' of the metric space ''M'' to itself. This distance measures how far the shapes ''X'' and ''Y'' are from being isometric.

The [[Gromov–Hausdorff convergence]] is a related idea: measuring the distance of two metric spaces ''M'' and ''N'' by taking the infimum of <math>d_\text{H}\big(I(M), J(N)\big)</math> among all isometric embeddings <math>I\colon M \to L</math> and <math>J\colon N \to L</math> into some common metric space ''L''.
